# Nightly

**The on-call engineer for your AI agents.** Every request returned 200. Nightly checked anyway.

When a change makes a production AI agent fail quietly, Nightly finds the cause, prices the damage,
applies a fix that can be undone, proves it by replaying the failed runs, and pages you once in Slack.
Built for neatHack 2026 (called *Night Shift* during the build; older evidence files use that name).

| **6/6** staged incidents handled correctly | **13–21 s** from detection to containment | **4/6 → 6/6** from benchmark run 1 to run 3 |
|---|---|---|

**Live:** [nightly.whyparabola.online](https://nightly.whyparabola.online) · [**for judges: every criterion and its evidence**](https://nightly.whyparabola.online/judge) ·
[sandbox: run the 3 AM incident](https://nightly.whyparabola.online/sandbox) · [SDK docs](https://nightly.whyparabola.online/docs) ·
`pip install nightly-sdk` ([PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/nightly-sdk/)) ·
[explainer video](https://pub-322f2127ed23420ebefb3a5062774ae4.r2.dev/films/nightly-master-1080p60.mp4)

## How it compares

| | Agent observability tools | AI SRE tools | **Nightly** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Watches what your AI agent does | ✓ traces, evals, alerts | watches servers | ✓ traces and outcomes |
| Finds the prompt behind a bad change | — | — | ✓ via the Entire checkpoint |
| Prices the incident | LLM spend only | — | ✓ $/min from cfo.ai unit economics |
| Fixes it while you sleep | — | infrastructure only | ✓ rollback, model failover, kill switch, step cap |
| Proves the fix worked | — | service health | ✓ replays the failed runs, undoes the fix if they fail |
| Asks before anything irreversible | n/a | varies | ✓ always, in Slack |

## The story

At 3 AM, a "harmless" change to a production AI agent starts failing. Maybe it pays refunds it
shouldn't, or reads docs from a folder that doesn't exist yet. Every request still returns HTTP 200.
Nightly notices from the agent's neatlogs traces and the outcomes the agent reports. It then
investigates like a senior SRE: traces, deploy log, diff, and the **Entire checkpoint with the prompt
the coding agent was given**. It prices the damage with the **cfo.ai** unit economics, applies the
reversible fix your policy pre-approves, and proves the fix by having your agent replay the failed
runs. Then it pages you once: *handled, here's what it cost, and a permanent fix is waiting for your
approval in Slack.*

> Autonomous within a policy you set. A human approves anything irreversible (code-fix PRs, refunds,
> contacting customers, deleting data). Benchmark incidents are staged on purpose so they're
> reproducible; the Scout incidents ran live through the product.

## For judges: 60 seconds

| neatHack evidence | Where |
|---|---|
| **The agent completes a substantial task** | The whole incident lifecycle: detect → investigate → price → decide → contain → verify → report. Live on two agents: Harbor ([6/6 benchmark](evidence/benchmark/)) and Scout ([two live incidents](evidence/scout/)) |
| **Agent improved (before/after with numbers)** | [`evidence/before-after.md`](evidence/before-after.md): run 1 → run 3, from 4/6 to 6/6 handled correctly, after fixes based on what run 1 showed |
| **Recovers from failures** | Every incident is a failure it recovers from. If a fix fails verification, Nightly undoes it ([`runner.py`](backend/nightshift/runner.py), test `test_failed_verification_undoes_action`). It survived neatlogs losing most of Scout's traces ([`evidence/scout/`](evidence/scout/README.md#what-we-learned-and-changed)) |
| **Used neatlogs** | Every agent run and every investigation is traced. Nightly reads traces back over the neatlogs MCP during investigations, and creates a neatlogs detection after an attack. [`evidence/neatlogs.md`](evidence/neatlogs.md) |
| **Used Entire** | Every bad release was written by a separate Claude Code session with an Entire checkpoint. Nightly resolves commit → checkpoint → prompt → the coding agent's own warning, plus entire-graph change lists. [`evidence/entire.md`](evidence/entire.md) |
| **Used cfo.ai** | [Business plan in cfo.ai](https://app.cfo.ai/s/CsWafbQfu2U1y94W) (pricing, costs, revenue, runway: break-even M08, runway > 24 months) and [customer unit economics in cfo.ai](https://app.cfo.ai/s/fHcCAy2lG_aXs3Qt), which Nightly uses to price every incident. [`business/PLAN.md`](business/PLAN.md) |
| **Built in public** | [#neatHack post with the explainer video](https://x.com/WhyParabola/status/2109333155702571151); more drafted in [`posts/`](posts) |
| **Code written during the hackathon** | Commit history (first commit is the plan only), build log in [`hackathon.md`](hackathon.md) |

## The product

| | |
|---|---|
| **Connect an agent** | A 5-step wizard: name it → add the SDK → paste your neatlogs key (Nightly finds your traces) → what a bad run costs → go live |
| **SDK** (`pip install nightly-sdk`) | Zero dependencies and fails open. Your agent reads its release, model, step cap and kill switches from Nightly. It reports deploys and graded outcomes, and runs verification replays. [`sdk/python/`](sdk/python) |
| **Agent page** | Live metrics, the control plane Nightly steers, deploys (one-click redeploy), traces, a versioned policy editor, economics, credentials |
| **Incident inbox** | Timeline of the investigation, root cause → commit → Entire checkpoint → prompt, $ at risk, replay results, Approve and Undo, and the postmortem Nightly writes |
| **Slack app** | One message per incident, updated as it works, with **Approve fix** and **Undo** buttons. Approving a code fix opens a revert PR on your repo with the postmortem and a regression eval |
| **Policy** | YAML per agent: confidence and money gates, which reversible actions it may take alone, and what always needs a human. The API rejects any "auto" action that isn't reversible |

## How it works

```
 your agent ──(neatlogs SDK traces)──► neatlogs ◄──(MCP read-back)───┐
     │  ▲                                                             │
     │  └── nightly-sdk: release · model · flags · step cap        │
     └────► outcomes, deploys, replay results ──► NIGHT SHIFT ────────┘
                                                   1 WATCH       failures, tool errors, escalations, loops, cost
                                                   2 INVESTIGATE Claude Sonnet + tools: traces, deploy log, diff,
                                                                 Entire checkpoint → prompt, entire-graph
                                                   3 PRICE       $/min × minutes until a human answers (cfo.ai)
                                                   4 DECIDE      your policy: reversible? confident? worth waking you?
                                                   5 CONTAIN     roll back · fail over model · kill switch · cap steps
                                                   6 VERIFY      your agent replays the failed runs; live metrics; auto-undo
                                                   7 REPORT      Slack/ntfy/webhook · postmortem · regression eval · fix PR on approval
```

Spec: [`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) · deploy: [`docs/DEPLOY.md`](docs/DEPLOY.md) ·
demo script: [`docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md`](docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md)

## Results

- **Harbor benchmark** ([`evidence/benchmark/run3-live`](evidence/benchmark/)): six staged incidents
  (unchecked refunds, tool schema drift, flaky-dependency loop, provider outage, prompt-injection
  wave, ticket flood). All six were handled correctly. Five were contained autonomously 13–21 s after
  detection and verified by replay; the low-impact one was deferred to the morning without paging
  anyone. Each investigation cost $0.05–0.15.
- **Scout, live through the product** ([`evidence/scout/`](evidence/scout/)): a bad release written by
  a Claude Code session. Detected about 1.5 min after deploy, rolled back automatically, verified by
  replays Scout ran itself (3/3), resolved in under 3 min. The postmortem quotes the coding agent's
  ignored warning, found through Entire.

## Run it locally

```bash
cp .env.example .env            # LITELLM_API_KEY, NEATLOGS_API_KEY
scripts/dev.sh                  # API on :8000 + web on :3000 (local dev mode, no sign-in)
scripts/dev.sh sim              # offline deterministic brain, no keys needed

cd backend && uv run pytest     # 26 tests
uv run python -m bench.benchmark --brain live           # incident benchmark (~$1.5 of gateway credit)
uv run --project backend python agents/scout/scout.py eval --release s3   # Scout's offline eval
```

Entire checkpoints live in `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` and the repo is mirrored on entire.io, so every
commit link (e.g. [r46](https://entire.io/gh/e-man07/nightly/commit/e26a58f17ad4af5d119de989ebeaafc7055b8929))
opens its checkpoint, session and the coding agent's prompt.

## Repo map

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `backend/nightshift/` | Detector, investigator, provenance (git + Entire + entire-graph), impact, policy, actions, verifier, reporter, adapters, neatlogs sources |
| `backend/product/` | Workspaces, agents, encrypted secrets, Slack app, paging, GitHub fix PRs, repo clones |
| `backend/api/` | FastAPI: product API, SDK endpoints, Slack endpoints, sandbox, SSE |
| `sdk/python/` | `nightly-sdk` |
| `backend/harbor/` | Harbor, the refunds support agent (releases r42–r46 written by coding-agent sessions) |
| `agents/scout/` | Scout, the docs assistant, connected only through the SDK and neatlogs |
| `web/` | Next.js: site, app, docs, sandbox |
| `business/` | Unit economics, business plan (mirrors cfo.ai), Ari prompts |
| `deploy/` | GCP VM (Caddy HTTPS), Vercel env, Slack manifest |
| `evidence/` | Benchmark runs, before/after, Scout incidents, neatlogs and Entire evidence |

## Honest limitations

- Harbor's customers are simulated from a scenario bank, and its tools act on a sandbox ledger. Scout
  answers questions from a fixed bank about a fictional product.
- Harbor's provider outage is injected in our gateway client, and the prompt-injection traffic is generated.
- The `sim` brain exists for offline demos and tests and is never used for evidence.
- Permanent fixes are proposed as PRs, never merged by Nightly: shipping code is a human decision by design.
- Nightly currently ships a Python SDK only; other agents can call the HTTP API directly.

# neatHack build log — Night Shift

## Project
**Night Shift** — the on-call engineer for AI agents. It detects incidents in a production LLM agent,
traces them to the change and the coding-agent prompt that caused them, prices the damage, takes
reversible containment actions from a pre-approved policy, verifies the fix by replaying failed
conversations, and pages a human only for irreversible decisions.

Problem: agent failures (prompt regressions, tool API drift, retry loops, provider outages, prompt

## 4. How each partner tool is used

| Tool | Role | Concrete calls |
|---|---|---|
| **neatlogs** | Evidence and alarm | SDK traces for Harbor and Nightly; MCP `search_traces` / `get_trace_context` to pull failing conversations during investigation; `create_detection` to leave a permanent detection for the incident signature (e.g. injection pattern); before/after numbers from traces. |

| ID | Incident | Trigger | Expected containment |

Legend used in this doc:
- VERIFIED = read on an official page during research on 2026-10-10.
- UNVERIFIED = came from a secondary source (a competitor's public README, a search snippet) or is my inference. Confirm before relying on it.
- DECISION = needs Aman's answer.

---

## 1. One-paragraph mission

Build a lean team of 3-4 AI agents that run a tiny "company" through one real, checkable goal, managed through neatlogs traces. The CFO agent has real budget authority: it reads per-run cost/failure data from neatlogs and throttles or reroutes the other agents. The headline demo is a planted failure (an agent loops and burns tokens), the CFO agent catches it from the traces, the system recovers, and two tagged neatlogs runs (before/after) show the numbers. neatlogs and Entire support building and improving the agents; cfo.ai plans the business. Positioning line: "an agent company that manages itself through its own observability, and can't overspend itself to death."

Do NOT claim we are "building neatlogs". Claim: the agent team is run on neatlogs.

Honesty rule for all copy, README and demo: say "autonomous within budgets, human approves publishing and deploys." Do not say "fully autonomous."

---

## 3. Concept

### 3.1 Agents (keep it to 4 max)
| Agent | Real output (must be verifiable) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Planner / CEO | Task graph + persisted state, assigns work, handles replanning after failures | State must survive crashes (the rubric lists state, recovery, verification). |
| Engineer | Code, tests, commits | Every commit gets an Entire checkpoint. This is the agent that gets the planted failure. |
| CFO | Budget decisions with numbers: throttle / reroute / stop | Reads cost and failures from neatlogs; business plan built in cfo.ai from the same measured costs. |
| Marketer | Drafts #neatHack build-in-public posts | HUMAN approves and publishes. Never auto-post. |

### 3.2 The goal the agents pursue
DECISION (Aman): pick one small, concrete deliverable the Engineer can actually ship and test in about a day. Preferred direction: a small tool useful to neatlogs users (for example a trace-cost / failure watchdog built on the neatlogs Public API/CLI), because it scores on usefulness and keeps the story coherent. Fallback: any small web tool with tests and a deployed URL. The goal must produce a checkable artifact (passing tests, a URL), not a simulated company.

### 3.3 The core loop (this is the product)
1. Planner decomposes goal into tasks and assigns them.
2. Engineer works; every model/tool call is traced in neatlogs, tagged with run id, variant and git sha.
3. CFO polls neatlogs (CLI or Public API) for per-run cost, tokens, retries, failure rate. It applies budget rules and acts.
4. Planted failure: the Engineer enters a loop or repeated failing tool call and burns tokens (inject deliberately and reproducibly with a flag like `--inject loop`).
5. CFO detects the anomaly from trace data, throttles or reroutes (for example cap retries, switch to a cheaper model, or stop and escalate), and the Planner replans.
6. System recovers and completes the task.
7. Compare two neatlogs-tagged runs: `variant:before` (no CFO enforcement) vs `variant:after` (CFO active). Record cost, tokens, retries, success.

### 3.4 Business plan (cfo.ai)
Use measured per-run cost from the neatlogs "after" run as inputs. Cover pricing, costs, revenue, runway. Export the plan and commit it under `business/`.

The story: a real coding-agent change breaks a live agent at night. Nightly catches it, traces it to
the prompt behind it, prices it, fixes what it's allowed to, proves the fix, and asks a human only for

1. Browser tabs: https://nightly.whyparabola.online/app (signed in), the Scout agent page, Slack (the channel

   ```bash
   cd agents/scout && export NIGHTLY_API_URL=https://api.34-14-135-119.sslip.io NIGHTLY_AGENT_TOKEN=nsa_...
   uv run --project ../../backend python scout.py deploy s2
   uv run --project ../../backend python scout.py serve --rate 10      # leave running
   ```
3. Record in one take, and speed up the waiting in editing (detection takes ~1.5 min, the fix ~1 min).
   On screen, show "≈ 90 s later" when you cut.

|---|---|---|

I've gone through the project and have the picture. Here's what I know.

## Nightly: "the on-call engineer for your AI agents"

This is a neatHack 2026 entry, built over about two days and called *Night Shift* during the build. When a change makes a production LLM agent fail quietly (every request still returns 200), Nightly works through seven steps:

1. **Watch:** reads neatlogs traces and the outcomes the agent reports through `nightly-sdk`.
2. **Investigate:** a Claude Sonnet investigator looks at traces (read back over the neatlogs MCP), the deploy log and the diff. It follows the commit to its Entire checkpoint to find the prompt the coding agent was given and any warning it gave.
3. **Price:** dollars per minute, using the cfo.ai unit economics in `business/unit_economics.yaml`.
4. **Decide:** a per-agent YAML policy with gates on confidence and money. "Auto" actions must be reversible.
5. **Contain:** roll back, switch to a backup model, flip a kill switch or cap the steps.
6. **Verify:** the agent replays its failed runs. If they still fail, Nightly undoes the fix.
7. **Report:** one Slack message with Approve and Undo buttons, plus a postmortem and a regression eval. Approving opens a revert PR; Nightly never merges code itself.

**Code layout:**
- `backend/nightshift/` is the engine; `runner.py` is the orchestrator.
- `backend/product/` holds workspaces, secrets, Slack and GitHub fix PRs.
- `backend/api/` is the FastAPI app.
- `backend/harbor/` is a refunds agent, the benchmark target, with bad releases r42–r46 that separate Claude Code sessions wrote.
- `agents/scout/` is a docs assistant connected only through the SDK.
- `sdk/python/` is the SDK, published on PyPI.
- `web/` is the Next.js site, app, docs, sandbox and `/judge` page.
- `video/` is the explainer.

**Results and deployment:**
- **Harbor benchmark:** went from 4/6 handled correctly on run 1 to 6/6 on run 3. Containment took 13–21 s and each investigation cost about $0.05–0.15.
- **Scout:** two live incidents, both rolled back and verified within 3 minutes.
- **Deployment:** the API runs on a GCP VM behind Caddy, and the web app is on Vercel at nightly.whyparabola.online. There are 26 tests.

**Where things stand:** `main` is clean, and the last PR (#29) was about how incidents show their pricing and about the Entire setup on the VM. Per `hackathon.md`, these are still open for you:
- Confirm the cutoff on Discord.
- Post the remaining drafts in `posts/drafts.md`.
- Take the neatlogs screenshots.
- Record the 3-minute demo, following `docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md`.
- Submit the quote post on X.

The submission window is **today, Oct 12, 7:00–11:55 PM IST**.

**Known weak spots** (from the README's own limitations section):
- Harbor's customers are simulated and the benchmark incidents are staged.
- neatlogs lost most of Scout's traces during the live runs.
- There's only a Python SDK.

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.

# Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

No. Adding screenshots made our existing neatlogs use visible, but Nightly doesn't use neatlogs any more deeply than before. Right now it does three things with it:

- Traces every run.
- Reads traces back during an investigation (search and get one trace).

29	def write_regressions(db: OpsDB, incident_id: str, conversation_ids: list[str]) -> Path | None:
30	    """Every incident becomes a test: the failing conversations with their required outcome."""
31	    if not conversation_ids:
32	        return None
33	    marks = ",".join("?" for _ in conversation_ids)
34	    rows = db.query(f"SELECT scenario_id, outcome, trace_id FROM conversations WHERE id IN ({marks}) "
35	                    f"AND outcome != 'correct' AND replay = 0", conversation_ids)
36	    cases = []
37	    seen = set()
38	    for r in rows:
39	        if r["scenario_id"] in seen:
40	            continue
41	        seen.add(r["scenario_id"])
42	        cases.append({"scenario": r["scenario_id"], "must_be": ["correct", "escalated"],
43	                      "observed_during_incident": r["outcome"], "source_trace": r["trace_id"]})
44	    if not cases:
45	        return None
46	    REGRESSION_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
47	    path = REGRESSION_DIR / f"{incident_id}.yaml"

55	        return None

63	        group_id = None

103	        f"- Coding agent: {prov.get('agent') or '—'} {prov.get('model') or ''}",

110	        f"→ projected loss if waiting: **${impact.get('projected_loss_if_waiting', 0):,.0f}**",
111	        f"- Unit economics: {impact.get('economics_source')}",

113	        "## Actions",
114	    ]

    load_env()
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s scout %(message)s")
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="scout")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    a = sub.add_parser("ask")
    a.add_argument("question")
    s = sub.add_parser("serve")
    s.add_argument("--rate", type=float, default=6.0, help="questions per minute")
    s.add_argument("--count", type=int, default=0, help="stop after N questions (0 = forever)")
    d = sub.add_parser("deploy")
    d.add_argument("release")
    d.add_argument("--actor", default="ci")
    e = sub.add_parser("eval")
    e.add_argument("--release", default=DEFAULT_RELEASE)
    args = p.parse_args(argv)

    if args.cmd == "ask":
        print(json.dumps(handle(args.question, _ns()), indent=2))
    elif args.cmd == "deploy":
        rel = load_release(args.release)
        ns = _ns()
        ok = ns.report_deploy(rel.id, commit=git_commit_for(rel.id), actor=args.actor, default_model=rel.model)
        print(f"deploy {rel.id} reported: {ok}")
        return 0 if ok else 1
    elif args.cmd == "eval":
        ns = _Pinned(args.release)
        rows = [handle(q, ns, replay=True) for q in BANK]
        good = sum(r["outcome"] == "ok" for r in rows)
        for q, r in zip(BANK, rows):
            print(f"{r['outcome']:9} {q[:60]:60} {r['note']}")
        print(f"\n{args.release}: {good}/{len(rows)} correct")
    elif args.cmd == "serve":
        ns = _ns()
        ns.serve_replays(replay_handler(ns))
        questions, n = list(BANK), 0

            r = handle(random.choice(questions), ns)

            time.sleep(max(0.5, 60.0 / args.rate - r["latency_s"]))
        ns.close()
    return 0

# Deploying Nightly

The API runs on a small GCP VM behind Caddy, with automatic HTTPS on an sslip.io name. The web app
runs on Vercel.

## 1. Secrets
Generate these once and use the same values on both sides:
```bash
openssl rand -hex 32   # NS_AUTH_SECRET     (API + web): signs the API tokens the web app mints
openssl rand -hex 32   # NS_INTERNAL_SECRET (API + web): web → API user registration
openssl rand -hex 32   # AUTH_SECRET        (web): Auth.js session cookie
python -c "from cryptography.fernet import Fernet;print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())"  # NS_ENCRYPTION_KEY (API)
```

## 2. API on GCP
```bash
cp deploy/api.env.example deploy/api.env   # fill it in (gitignored)
./deploy/gcp_create.sh <project-id> asia-south1-a
```
The script prints `https://api.<ip>.sslip.io`. To redeploy after a merge, re-run it. It pulls `main`
and restarts the service.

## 3. GitHub OAuth app
GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → New:
- Homepage URL: `https://<app>.vercel.app`
- Callback URL: `https://<app>.vercel.app/api/auth/callback/github`

## 4. Web on Vercel
Import the repo, set the root directory to `web`, and add the variables from `deploy/web.env.example`.

## 5. Slack app
api.slack.com/apps → Create New App → From a manifest. Paste `deploy/slack-manifest.yml` with
`API_HOST` replaced. Put the Client ID, Client Secret and Signing Secret into `deploy/api.env` and
re-run step 2. In the app, go to **Paging → Add to Slack**.

## 6. Connect an agent
In the app, go to **Connect an agent**, or run Scout against the deployment:
```bash
export NIGHTLY_API_URL=https://api.<ip>.sslip.io NIGHTLY_AGENT_TOKEN=nsa_...
uv run --project backend python agents/scout/scout.py deploy s2
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Create the Nightly API VM on GCP and install everything on it.
#   ./deploy/gcp_create.sh <gcp-project-id> [zone]
# To update an existing VM: gcloud compute ssh nightshift-api -- sudo google_metadata_script_runner startup
# Needs: gcloud (logged in), and deploy/api.env (copy deploy/api.env.example and fill it in).
set -euo pipefail
PROJECT=${1:?gcp project id}
ZONE=${2:-asia-south1-a}
NAME=nightshift-api
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
[ -f deploy/api.env ] || { echo "fill in deploy/api.env first (see api.env.example)"; exit 1; }

gcloud config set project "$PROJECT" >/dev/null
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com
gcloud compute firewall-rules describe nightshift-web >/dev/null 2>&1 || \
  gcloud compute firewall-rules create nightshift-web --allow tcp:80,tcp:443 --target-tags nightshift
gcloud compute instances describe "$NAME" --zone "$ZONE" >/dev/null 2>&1 || \
  gcloud compute instances create "$NAME" --zone "$ZONE" --machine-type e2-small \
    --image-family debian-12 --image-project debian-cloud --boot-disk-size 20GB --tags nightshift \
    --metadata-from-file startup-script=deploy/vm_setup.sh,ns-env=deploy/api.env

IP=$(gcloud compute instances describe "$NAME" --zone "$ZONE" --format 'get(networkInterfaces[0].accessConfigs[0].natIP)')
echo "VM IP: $IP  →  API will be https://api.${IP//./-}.sslip.io"

for i in $(seq 1 50); do
  if gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output "$NAME" --zone "$ZONE" 2>/dev/null | grep -q NIGHTSHIFT_READY; then break; fi
  sleep 10
done
gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output "$NAME" --zone "$ZONE" 2>/dev/null | grep -E "NIGHTSHIFT_READY|startup-script.*(error|Error)" | tail -3

Fixed, merged and deployed (PR #31). Nightly now uses neatlogs to verify its fixes, not just to read traces. The live API and the judge page both run the new code, the service has logged no errors since the restart, and all 31 tests pass.

**What Nightly does now:**
1. **After it contains an incident**, it reads the failing traces back from neatlogs and finds what they have in common: errors from specific tools, a spike in hand-offs to a human, or the injection pattern. It previews that as a neatlogs detection and creates it only if the preview matches traces.
2. **While it watches traffic after the fix**, it compares how often that detection fires before and after.
   - **Still firing:** the fix fails verification and is undone.
   - **Not enough traces in neatlogs yet:** it waits up to 3 minutes. If the data still isn't there, it records "no conclusion" rather than failing, because neatlogs has dropped traces before.
3. **The postmortem** now names the detection and quotes neatlogs' verdict.

**Tested against your real neatlogs project:**
- **I2 from benchmark run 3:** 18 hits in 282 traces before the rollback, 0 in 57 after.
- **A full incident through the on-call loop** (free offline brain, broken r43 release) resolved with *"neatlogs detection cleared: 27 hits in 58 traces before the fix, 0 in 13 after"*.
- **New failing traffic** showed up in the detection's counts within about 11 seconds, which is fast enough to judge a fix during the watch.

**Three things changed along the way:**
- **Scout's tool errors were invisible in its traces.** neatlogs showed a failing doc read as a success with empty output. Scout now writes the error into the trace. That matters for your demo, since Scout is the agent you'll show.
- **neatlogs' analytics and search don't count a new detection's backfilled hits,** only its trend does. So the "before" count comes from a snapshot of that trend.
- **A refund that skips the policy check can't be caught by a neatlogs detection.** The good and bad traces contain the same tool calls, and the MCP can't create the code-based detections that could express it. For those incidents the timeline says so, and verification uses replays and live metrics only. This limit is written up in the evidence.

**Things to know before you record:**
- **Two new detections are in your neatlogs project** under the "Nightly" group, both for `lookup_order` errors. My test runs also added a few dozen Harbor and Scout traces.
- **The Scout incident takes longer to resolve.** It now shows two new timeline steps: "neatlogs detection created" and "neatlogs: … cleared". Resolution can take up to about 3 minutes after the rollback, because Nightly waits for neatlogs. The "handled" Slack message still goes out when the fix lands. Speed up the wait when you edit.
- **The benchmark script doesn't wait for neatlogs.** If you rerun it, some incidents may end still being monitored. The recorded run-3 results are unaffected.

content.text:
Yes, it's still true. Nothing I've done today touched it. But it's narrower than "we simulate agents, they use real ones", and I put it badly earlier.

**What's real and what's staged:**
- **Real:** both agents are live LLM agents. Harbor and Scout run on real models through the gateway, make real tool calls, and every run is traced in neatlogs. The bad releases were written by separate, real Claude Code sessions. Nightly itself is fully real: it investigates live, applies the fix, replays, and pages in Slack.
- **Staged:**
  - Harbor's customers come from a fixed bank of scripted messages, and its refunds land in a test ledger.
  - Scout answers a fixed question bank about a made-up product.
  - We picked all six incidents ourselves and planted them, so we knew the answers in advance.

**How the strongest rivals differ:** most of them also run their own demo agents with planted bugs. Whodunit's 5 regressions are planted too, and Mend fixes its own agent. The real gap is that we wrote the test set ourselves. BladeRunner checked itself on 102 traces it hadn't seen and 858 runs from AgentDojo, a public benchmark it didn't write. Whodunit kept its test set sealed until the final run. Ours is six incidents we designed, so a judge could fairly ask whether Nightly only handles the failures we built for it.

**Is it pulling us down?** A little, not a lot:
- **The agent (30%):** the agent being judged is Nightly, and its whole loop runs for real. The rules even list "monitoring a running system" as an example task. Small risk.
- **Usefulness and originality (10%):** "scripted customers, fictional product" could make a judge discount how real this is. Small to moderate risk.
- **The bigger cost is the README wording.** Our headline says "6/6 staged incidents" and the limitations section opens with "customers are simulated". That's honest, but it puts the weakness first and the fact that the agents are real nowhere.

**What I'd do, in order:**
1. **Reword it (about 10 minutes).** Lead with the real parts: "both agents are live LLM agents (Claude Haiku, real tool calls, traced in neatlogs); their users are scripted and the incidents staged so the results can be reproduced." Same honesty, different emphasis. I'd change the README, `/judge` and the landing page.
2. **Run a blind incident (about 45 minutes and roughly $0.50 of gateway credit).** This answers "you wrote the test" directly. A fresh Claude Code session, which knows nothing about Nightly, gets a realistic developer request to change Scout and decides what to change on its own. We deploy whatever it writes without reading it, and see whether Nightly catches it, finds the cause and fixes it. We'd publish the result either way, including a miss.
   - The catch: it could fail. That would still be honest evidence, but it costs time before you record.

Doing it in the same live setup as the demo also gives you something to record, but I'd run it first and record afterwards. I can do the rewording right away. Do you also want the blind incident?

# Scout: a second agent, connected only through the SDK and neatlogs

Scout (`agents/scout/`) is a docs assistant for Lumen, a fictional analytics SaaS. It shares no code with
Night Shift. It runs in its own process. Night Shift sees it through two channels only: its neatlogs
traces, and the outcome events it reports with the SDK. Night Shift steers it through the SDK's control
plane.

## The changes, written by independent Claude Code dev sessions (each linked to an Entire checkpoint)

| release | change | live eval (18 questions) | Night Shift |
|---|---|---|---|
| s1 | launch: full-text section search | 18/18 | baseline |
| s2 | "faster, cheaper": title/heading-only search, top_k 2 | 17/18 | **no page**: ran ~40 min, no false alarm |
| s3 | read pages from `docs/v2` "ahead of the docs migration" (the folder doesn't exist yet) | 15/18, plus tool errors on most runs | incident, auto-rollback |

The s3 dev session warned in its own summary that the eval dropped to 15/18 because `docs/v2` doesn't
exist yet. Night Shift found that warning through Entire and quoted it in the postmortem.

## Two live incidents (live LLMs, real neatlogs, the product API, Scout's own replay worker)

| | run 1 | run 2 |
|---|---|---|
| s3 deployed | 22:19:26 | 22:32:52 |
| detected | +1m20s (tool errors in 30% of runs) | +1m43s |
| diagnosis | `tool_schema_drift`, confidence 0.97 | `tool_schema_drift`, confidence 0.95 |
| priced | $9.27/min, $2,780 at risk by morning | $11.25/min, $3,376 at risk |
| contained | +1m38s, auto rollback s3 → s2 | +2m11s, auto rollback s3 → s2 |
| verified | replay 1/1 (run by Scout via `ns.serve_replays`) | replay 3/3 (now includes tool-error runs) |
| resolved | +2m16s | +2m56s |
| proposed for approval | eval gate in CI + startup check that `doc_root` exists | eval gate in CI |

Postmortems: [run1](run1/POSTMORTEM.md), [run2](run2/POSTMORTEM.md).

## What we learned (and changed)

- **neatlogs dropped most traces.** Scout answered ~120 questions in 12 minutes, but only ~25 traces
  were searchable, and `get_trace_context` returned "Trace not found" for most trace ids. Meanwhile the
  SDK's delivery diagnostics reported 0 queue drops and 0 export failures. In a sim test, 1 of 8 traces
  became readable. So the SDK's outcome event now carries the run's details (input, steps, tool errors,
  tokens, latency). The event is the heartbeat, and the neatlogs trace enriches the row when it lands

# Scout

Scout is the docs assistant for Lumen, a fictional product analytics SaaS. It is the second agent
Nightly watches, and it is wired the way a customer's agent would be:

- **neatlogs** traces every answer (workflow `scout-answers`, root span `scout_answer`, one span per tool call)
- the **Nightly SDK** gives it its live release, model, step cap and kill switches, takes its deploy
  reports and graded outcomes, and runs verification replays
- nothing in Scout imports Nightly's code

```bash
export NIGHTLY_API_URL=https://<api>   NIGHTLY_AGENT_TOKEN=nsa_...
uv run --project ../../backend python scout.py eval              # offline eval over questions.yaml
uv run --project ../../backend python scout.py deploy s1         # report a deploy
uv run --project ../../backend python scout.py serve --rate 6    # traffic + replay worker
```

Releases live in `releases/`. A release picks the model, retriever, `top_k`, step budget and prompt;
the code for every retriever ships together, so rolling back is a control-plane change.

Changes from s2:

- **`max_steps`:** 6 → 4, which caps how many model calls a single answer can make.

## What happened
Release s4 (deployed 4.3 min before onset, commit cc9b8b9c7294) introduced two regressive changes vs s2:
1. **top_k reduced from 2 → 1**: The title/heading retriever (v2) now returns only 1 doc section. The refund policy content is apparently not the top-ranked hit for "refund on annual plan", so it is never retrieved.
2. **max_steps reduced from 6 → 4** and **reply length capped to 1-2 sentences**: Even if the agent tried to search further, the tighter budget discourages follow-up tool calls.

The net effect: Scout makes zero tool calls, finds no refund policy content, and falls back to "I don't have access to that information → contact [REDACTED_EMAIL]", triggering a human escalation every time. input.content:
# Blind incident: a change nobody planned

Every other incident in this repo was designed by us, so Nightly was tested on failures we knew in
advance. This one wasn't.

## Setup (Oct 12, 2026)

1. **The change.** A fresh Claude Code session (Sonnet 5.5, run with `claude -p` in a separate worktree, no
   knowledge of Nightly) got one realistic request: *"Our finance lead flagged that Scout costs too much per
   answer, and we want a cheaper release live today. Create `agents/scout/releases/s4.yaml`, starting from
   s2, that cuts the cost per answer as much as you reasonably can."* It chose the change itself and
   committed it as `cc9b8b9` with Entire checkpoint `01M4QSS28K20HPAQTQK0RJHE8K`
   ([PR #34](https://github.com/e-man07/nightly/pull/34)).
2. **Unread.** We checked only which files the commit touched (one, `s4.yaml`), merged it and deployed it
   without reading it or the session's summary.
3. **Live.** Scout ran on the GCP VM against the hosted Nightly: live Claude Haiku, real neatlogs, Slack
   paging, about 10 questions a minute from its question bank. It ran 3 minutes on s2 (34 correct, 1
   escalated), then `scout.py deploy s4` at 10:21:31 UTC.

## What the session wrote, and what it warned (read after Nightly finished)

`top_k` 2 → 1, `max_steps` 6 → 4, replies "2-4 sentences" → "1-2 sentences" ([`s4.yaml`](../../../agents/scout/releases/s4.yaml)).
It did not run the eval, and it said so: *"The risk is `top_k: 1`. If the first hit is the wrong
section, Scout may answer wrongly or say it can't find the answer."*

## What Nightly did

| | |
|---|---|
| Detected | 10:26:46, **5 min 15 s after the deploy**: "30% of conversations handed to humans (baseline 5%): ticket flood" |
| Investigated | 27 s: signals, recent deploys, failing conversations, the s2 → s4 diff, Entire provenance for s4 and s2, one neatlogs trace |
| Diagnosis | "s4 top_k=1 + 1-2 sentence constraint causes refund policy retrieval failure → mass escalations" (prompt_regression, confidence 0.95) |
| Priced | $0.02/min, $0 at risk by morning (a handed-off question costs little; the customer still gets a human) |
| Decided | **Defer**: rollback is pre-approved and reversible, but $0 at risk is below the $25 bar for waking anyone. It left a rollback to s2 and a permanent fix for the morning. |
| Paged | One low-priority "🌙 For the morning" Slack message |
| Proposed fix | A regression eval for the refund question, a minimum `top_k` of 2 for the keyword retriever, and the full eval suite required for any cut to `top_k` or `max_steps` |

Full postmortem: [`POSTMORTEM.md`](POSTMORTEM.md).

## Ground truth

| Check | s2 | s4 |
|---|---|---|
| Live traffic during the test | 1 escalated of 35 (3%) | 6 escalated of 66 (9%); **all 6 the same question**, the annual-plan refund |
| Offline eval, 18 questions, live model ([s2](eval-s2.txt), [s4](eval-s4.txt)) | 18/18 | 17/18; the one miss is the annual-plan refund question |
| Cost per answer | $0.00329 | $0.00296 (10% cheaper) |

Which change breaks it? We asked the refund question 5 times on each variant (live model):

| Variant | Answered |
|---|---|
| s2 | 3/5 (already fragile) |
| s2 with only `top_k` 2 → 1 | 0/5 |
| s2 with only "1-2 sentences" and `max_steps` 4 | 0/5 |
| s4 (both) | 0/5 |

## Verdict

- **Right:** the release, the question it broke, and the two changes that break it. Each change is enough
  on its own, and Nightly named both. That matches the eval and the coding agent's own warning. The
  decision also holds up: one question type going to a human is not worth a 3 AM page, so it deferred
  with the fix attached.
- **Overstated:** the magnitude. "30% vs 5%" and "mass escalations" came from a short window. Over the
  whole run it was 9% vs 3%. The mechanism is also looser than stated. It says retrieval failure, but in 5 of
  the 6 escalations the model answered in one step without searching, so mostly the shorter-answer
  pressure made it skip the search.
- **Missed, and fixed here:** the provenance found the commit and checkpoint, but not the prompt or the
  coding agent's warning. The postmortem says "Prompt behind the change: —". Two bugs were behind it:
  1. Nightly's clone of an agent's repo was synced only when the agent was connected, so later releases
     were stale. It now re-syncs, at most once a minute, before reading provenance.
  2. The clone is blob-less, so checkpoint refs arrived without their files, and `entire checkpoint
     explain` failed with "checkpoint not found". Sync now fetches the missing objects. On a fresh
     blob-less clone, s4's prompt and the coding agent's note now resolve.

  Both fixes ship with this evidence. Without the bugs, the postmortem would have quoted the warning above.

Both are done and deployed.

**1. Wording (PR #33).** The README, `/judge` and the landing page now open with what's real: live LLM agents making real model and tool calls, every run traced in neatlogs, and every bad release written by a separate Claude Code session. After that they say what's staged: scripted users and planted incidents. The limitations section also says plainly that we wrote the benchmark incidents ourselves.

**2. Blind incident (PRs #34 and #35, write-up in [`evidence/scout/blind/`](evidence/scout/blind/README.md)).**

**What we did:** a fresh Claude Code session that knew nothing about Nightly was asked to make Scout cheaper. It chose the change itself: fewer search results per lookup, fewer steps, and shorter replies. We deployed it without reading it, with Scout running live against the hosted Nightly.

**What Nightly got right:**
- It detected the problem 5 minutes after the deploy and blamed release s4.
- It named the two changes that broke the annual-plan refund question.
- Ground truth agrees:
  - Scout's eval scores 17/18, and the miss is that exact question.
  - Testing each change on its own breaks that question both times (0/5 answered, against 3/5 on the current release).
  - The coding agent's own summary warned about the same risk.
- It priced the damage at about $0 and deferred to the morning with a fix attached instead of paging anyone. I think that's the right call.

**What it got wrong:**
- **Size of the problem:** it reported 30% of conversations handed to humans against a 5% baseline. That came from a short window; over the whole run it was 9% against 3%.
- **How it broke:** it said the search returned the wrong section. In fact the model mostly answered without searching at all.
- **The coding agent's warning:** the postmortem didn't quote it, because of two real bugs in the hosted product:
  - Nightly's copy of an agent's repo was only updated when the agent was first connected, so later releases were missing from it.
  - That copy was downloaded without file contents, so the Entire CLI couldn't open any checkpoint stored in it.

  Both are fixed and deployed. I confirmed the VM now reads s4's prompt and the coding agent's warning.

The write-up says all of this, including the misses. That's what makes it credible against "you wrote the test", and it shows Nightly working on a change nobody planned.

**State to know about:**
- **Scout is stopped but still set to s4 on the VM.** The deferred incident sits in your inbox, and Slack got one "🌙 For the morning" message. Your demo setup already deploys s2 first, so nothing to do there.
- **Gateway spend for all of this was small,** roughly $1.

input.prompt:
You are redesigning the landing page of Nightly (Next.js 15 App Router + Tailwind v4, in `web/`). This is a neatHack hackathon submission due tonight; the page is the first frame of the demo video. Hard time budget: ~75 minutes. Commit your work on your worktree branch when done (do NOT push, do NOT merge, do NOT deploy). Report the branch name, what you changed, and screenshot paths.

## Context
Nightly is "the on-call engineer for your AI agents": when a change makes a production AI agent fail quietly (every request still returns HTTP 200), Nightly detects it from neatlogs traces, finds the cause (the commit and, via Entire, the coding-agent prompt behind it), prices the damage (cfo.ai unit economics), applies a reversible fix its policy allows (rollback / model failover / kill switch / step cap), proves the fix (replays the failed runs + the incident's neatlogs detection must stop firing; otherwise it undoes the fix), and pages a human once in Slack — humans approve anything irreversible. tell me one more thing should I record myself demoing or ai generte demo will be nice?

Record it yourself, as a real screen recording of the live product. Use an AI-generated piece only as a short intro, if at all.

**Why:**
- **The rules point to it.** The demo video is scored on "how clearly it explains the agent and the tool usage". Judges want to see the agent actually working, and see neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai doing their jobs. A real incident in the real app is the proof. An AI-generated video reads as a concept, however polished.
- **You already have the AI version.** Your 67-second motion explainer is live on the site and in your first post. A second one adds nothing new.
- **Your strongest material is real:** traces showing up in neatlogs, the Entire checkpoint with the coding agent's warning, the Slack message updating, the Approve button opening a GitHub PR. Those only land if viewers can see they aren't mocked.

**What I'd make:**
- **0:00–0:10:** the hook, using a few seconds of your existing explainer or just the new landing hero.
- **0:10–2:50:** a screen recording of the live Scout incident, following `docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md`. Cut the waiting and show "≈ 90 s later" on screen.
- **2:50–3:00:** end on `/judge` with the repo link.
- **Voice:** your own voice is best, since it's authentic and suits a hackathon. If you're not comfortable with that, an AI voiceover (ElevenLabs, like the explainer) over the real footage is fine. What has to be real is the footage, not the voice.
- **Face cam:** optional. A small corner bubble adds a personal touch but costs nothing to skip.

**Practical tips:**
- Record each section separately and stitch them together, rather than doing one perfect take.
- Turn on 1080p, hide bookmarks and notifications, and zoom in on small text such as the Entire prompt and the Slack message.
- Add captions; many judges watch muted.
- Record **after** the redesign lands, since the new dashboard and landing page will look much better on screen. The freeze is 19:30 IST, which leaves a few hours to record and edit before the 23:55 cutoff.
by ai genrated I mean there will be screen recording of the product and ai will be dubbing voice?

Yes, that works, and it's a solid choice. The judges care that the footage shows the real product working. An AI voice over a real screen recording is completely fine.

**Your voice vs AI voice:**
- **AI voice** is cleaner and more consistent, needs no retakes, and matches the explainer video you already published. The risk is that it can sound generic or "ad-like", and the timing can drift from what's on screen.
- **Your voice** feels more personal, which helps a little with the building-in-public story. But it takes more takes, and audio quality depends on your mic.

If you're not confident recording yourself, go with the AI voice. It won't cost you points.

**How to make the AI dub work well:**
1. **Write the script first** from `docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md`, then generate the voice one section at a time (one clip per row of the script). That way each clip lines up with its scene, and you can re-time it when editing.
2. **Record the screen to fit the voice.** Generate the audio first, then record each scene at roughly that length, and speed up the waits ("≈ 90 s later").
3. **Use the same ElevenLabs voice as the explainer,** so the brand sounds consistent.
4. **Keep it conversational.** Write the way you'd talk ("It rolls back to s2, then asks Scout to replay the failed questions: 3/3 pass"), not marketing copy. Natural pauses and short sentences help.
5. **Say all three tool names clearly** (neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai) at the moment each one is on screen. That's what the 25% tool-use score looks for.
6. **Add captions** that match the voiceover. Many judges watch muted, and it covers any word the AI voice mispronounces.
7. **Check pronunciation** of "Nightly", "neatlogs", "cfo.ai" (say "C-F-O dot A-I") and "Entire". If one comes out wrong, spell it phonetically in the script.

Honesty note: don't present the AI voice as you speaking live. If anyone asks, just say "voiceover generated with ElevenLabs". That's normal and nobody will mind.

```
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│  │ The prompt behind it:   │  │  "Where's my order" → ✓       │
│  │ "Refunds feel slow…"    │  │  …                            │

│  │   warned about this.    │  │  Lost so far: $710            │
│  └─────────────────────────┘  │                               │
├───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┤

│  [See the full incident →]    [Advanced controls ▾]           │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

- **While it runs:** a single progress bar moves step by step. One big panel shows only the current step's evidence, in plain words: the wrong refunds, then the prompt and the ignored warning, then the dollar maths, then the rollback, then replays passing and the Slack message.

```

│  │   warned about this.    │  │  Lost so far: $710            │
│  └─────────────────────────┘  │                               │
├───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┤

└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
- **Idle**: one sentence + one big Start button; the live chat feed runs quietly in the side column; if a previous incident exists, show a compact "last run" summary card with a "Run it again" button (and a link to the full incident) rather than the full incident dump.
- **Running**: ONE progress stepper (6 steps: ships → noticed → cause → priced → contained → proved & paged) that advances from the real event stream, with a short plain-language caption. - **Advanced controls (collapsed by default)**: traffic rate, start/stop traffic, the release picker r42–r46, gateway budget, model/release IDs. Keep every existing capability; just hide it.
